# Professional Development

## Mentoring Philosophy

We believe in individualized mentoring that supports each person's unique career goals. Effective mentoring requires:

- Regular, open communication between mentees and mentors
- Mutual respect and trust
- Clear expectations and goals
- Constructive feedback
- Support for both research and career development

## Individual Development Plans

All graduate students and postdocs should maintain an Individual Development Plan (IDP) that outlines:

- Short-term and long-term career goals
- Skills to develop
- Training needs and opportunities
- Timeline and milestones
- Progress toward goals

Update your IDP at least annually and discuss it with your PI. Useful resources:

- [myIDP - Individual Development Plan tool](https://myidp.sciencecareers.org/)
- [NIH OITE Career Resources](https://www.training.nih.gov/career-services/)

## Presentations and Conferences

We encourage lab members to present their work at conferences and seminars:

- Discuss conference opportunities with PIs early
- Submit abstracts with PI approval
- Practice presentations in lab meeting before the conference
- Prioritize clear visuals over text-dense slides following our [Show, Don't Tell](@sec-show-dont-tell) principle
- Funding for conferences depends on availability and should be discussed in advance

### Guidelines for Slide Decks {#sec-slide-deck-guidelines}

When preparing slide presentations for lab meetings,
conferences, qualifying exams, or thesis defenses,
follow these practical guidelines:

- **Always include slide numbers**:
  Slide numbers are essential for receiving constructive feedback.
  During question-and-answer periods or practice feedback sessions,
  collaborators and audience members need to refer back to specific slides quickly
  (e.g., "On slide 14, how was that variable defined?")
  without fumbling through visual descriptions or guessing where a topic occurred.
- **Complete, record, and review practice runs**:
  Before any significant presentation,
  rehearse the complete talk out loud,
  record the practice run (using screen recording software, a webcam, or your phone),
  and review the recording.
  Watching your own practice run provides invaluable, objective feedback
  on pacing, timing, verbal filler habits, transition clarity,
  and whether slide text and figures remain legible when viewed on screen.
  Both students and faculty benefit substantially from this practice.
- **One primary takeaway per slide**:
  Limit the cognitive load of each slide.
  If a slide presents multiple distinct findings or complex arguments,
  split them across sequential slides so the audience can focus on each point.
- **Prioritize visual evidence**:
  Audiences cannot read dense paragraphs while simultaneously listening to a speaker.
  Favor clean charts, diagrams, and annotated figures over text-heavy bulleted lists.
- **Ensure high contrast and readability**:
  Use large, legible fonts and high-contrast color palettes.
  Verify that axis labels, legends, and annotations remain easily readable
  from the back of a large room or on low-resolution projector displays.

## Scientific Figures

Creating clear, effective figures is essential for communicating research findings:

- Label x-axis and y-axis clearly
- Use panel labels when including multiple subplots
- Include sufficient tick marks and labels
- Use appropriate font sizes (readable but not distracting)
- Use colorblind-friendly palettes (see [ColorBrewer](http://colorbrewer2.org/) or [iwanthue](https://medialab.github.io/iwanthue/))
- Define colors, shapes, and line types in legends
- Minimize abbreviations in labels and legends
- Use transparency to show overlapping data
- Show measures of precision (e.g., 95% confidence intervals)

**Resources:**

- [Ten Simple Rules for Better Figures](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003833)

## Grant Writing

- Graduate students and postdocs are encouraged to apply for fellowships (e.g., NIH F31, NSF GRFP, K awards)
- PIs will support fellowship applications with feedback, letters of support, and mentoring
- Start planning fellowship applications well in advance of deadlines (typically 3-6 months)
- Attend grant writing workshops and seek feedback from multiple sources

**Resources:**

- [Building Your Funding Train](https://grantwriting.stanford.edu/resources/funding-train/)
- [NIH Funding Opportunities](https://grants.nih.gov)
- [NIH Grant Writing Resources](https://www.niaid.nih.gov/grants-contracts/write-grant-application)

## Teaching and Outreach

Teaching and outreach are valuable professional development opportunities:

- Graduate students are encouraged to gain teaching experience
- We support science communication and outreach activities
- Discuss opportunities with PIs

The [UC Davis DataLab](https://github.com/ucdavisdatalab) offers various workshops and learning materials that can support your teaching and professional development. Their [workshop index](https://ucdavisdatalab.github.io/workshop_index/) provides a comprehensive catalog of available resources.

## Networking

Building a professional network is important for your career:

- Attend seminars and departmental events
- Connect with researchers in your field
- Join professional societies
- Use professional social media platforms to share research and engage with the scientific community
